title: An open specification for agentic AI security evaluation and testing, from Cisco
content:
An open specification for agentic AI security evaluation, from Cisco.
Cisco's Advanced Security Initiatives Group has built and operated an agentic security evaluation internally across several iterations and deployment models, and along the way accumulated a long list of design decisions that turned out to matter and a longer list that turned out not to.
Foundry distills that experience into a single, organization-neutral specification. It is the design that, across those iterations, consistently proved most effective. It is not our code. It is the shape of a system that works, with every lesson we learned written down as a requirement and every place where the right answer depends on your infrastructure left as an explicit open question.
You bring a frontier LLM and a target to evaluate. Foundry gives you the architecture, the invariants, and the guardrails. You build your own implementation, on your own stack, using the specification as the blueprint.
There is no code in this repository, and that is intentional. The specification is the deliverable.
Foundry's Detector role (§5.4) runs on a corpus of LLM-evaluated detection rules. The rule format we use is CodeGuard, which Cisco open-sourced well before Foundry existed and donated to the Coalition for Secure AI (CoSAI), where it is now maintained as an OASIS open project. Foundry did not invent CodeGuard; Foundry was designed to consume it, and to contribute back the one thing a static rule corpus cannot do for itself: grow from operational experience.
That contribution is the detection-to-prevention flywheel at the center of Foundry's design:
- Rules sweep every function in the target. Systematic, repeatable, finds what you already knew to look for.
- Exploratory agents hunt alongside. Creative, target-specific, finds what no rule describes yet.
- When exploration confirms something the rules missed, Foundry records a rule gap.
- The gap is generalized into a rule (a new one, or a revision of one that should have fired). The rule lands in the corpus.
- The next sweep, on this target and every future target, catches that whole class on the first pass. Exploration is freed to hunt further out.
- Repeat. There is no terminal state; every evaluation enlarges the corpus.
And because CodeGuard rules are portable, the same corpus loads into an LLM coding assistant as its secure-coding rule set: the bug class your last evaluation taught the corpus to detect is now prevented at the keystroke, in every developer's editor, before the next evaluation ever runs. Every turn of the loop improves detection here and prevention everywhere.
CodeGuard stands on its own and predates this work; you can run Foundry with a different rule format. What Foundry adds is the machinery that turns a rule corpus from a maintained artifact into a self-improving one.
Our internal systems are tightly coupled to Cisco's infrastructure: our cloud provider, our issue tracker, our LLM gateway, our deployment platform, our severity taxonomy. Open-sourcing that code would give you something that runs in exactly one environment: ours.
What transfers is the design: which agent roles you need and why, what each must guarantee, how findings flow from detection to publication, what "done" means for an evaluation, where the quality gates go, and which shortcuts will hurt you six months in. That design is infrastructure-neutral, and it is what this repository contains.
The specification is written to be consumed by spec-kit (or any spec-driven development workflow): you run it through a clarification step that resolves the open questions against your environment, and out the other side comes your spec, for your implementation, on your stack.
- Security teams with access to a frontier LLM, software they need to evaluate, and the question "how do we turn this model into a system that produces findings we can trust?"
- Platform and tooling teams building internal security-evaluation capabilities who would rather start from a proven shape than a blank page.
- Researchers studying AI-assisted vulnerability discovery who want a reference architecture grounded in production operation rather than benchmarks.
This is not a turnkey scanner. If you want something you can pip install and point at a repo today, this is not that. If you want to build the thing that your organization will still be running in three years, this is the blueprint.
- A coding agent that supports the spec-kit workflow (Claude Code or compatible).
- A repository where your implementation will live.
- Rough answers to: which LLM provider, which issue tracker, which datastore, where it will run. You don't need these finalized; the clarify step will walk you through them.
Open constitution.md and read it end to end. It is short. Each principle has a "why this is inviolable" paragraph describing the production failure that motivated it. If any principle seems wrong for your situation, the answer is more often "we have not hit that failure yet" than "that failure cannot happen here."
Follow the spec-kit installation instructions for your coding agent. At the end you should have a .specify/ directory in your project root and the /speckit.* commands available in your agent.
cp path/to/foundry/constitution.md  your-project/.specify/memory/constitution.md
Then run /speckit.constitution and indicate you are adopting an existing constitution. The agent will register it as the authority that later steps check against.
mkdir -p your-project/specs/001-foundry
cp path/to/foundry/spec.md  your-project/specs/001-foundry/spec.md/speckit.clarify
This is the step the seed was written for. The agent reads spec.md, finds every [NEEDS CLARIFICATION: ...] marker (around three dozen; §15 of the spec indexes them all), and walks you through them as questions. They fall into four groups:
Tips:
- "I do not know yet" is acceptable for integration and policy choices; the plan step will resurface them. It is not acceptable for identity and scope.
- When the seed says "the authors did X", that is one worked example, not a recommendation.
- When asked "merge, split, or omit", read the cost note at the end of that role's §5 section before answering.
At the end of clarify, your spec.md has been rewritten in place: markers replaced with your answers, dropped sections removed, a Clarifications log appended.
/speckit.specify
Hardens the clarified seed into a complete specification: expands sections your answers made necessary, renumbers FRs contiguously, verifies against the constitution, and sets status from SEED to DRAFT.
Read the result. This is now your specification. If anything in it reads as "someone else's system", clarify missed a question.
Specify can introduce new underspecification. In particular:
- If you said yes to any extension role in §6, specify just authored FRs for it from a one-paragraph sketch. Those FRs will almost certainly carry their own [NEEDS CLARIFICATION: ...] markers (e.g., for Attack-Mapper: which graph store, what node-id scheme, how are by-design edges sourced).
- An integration choice you made can expose follow-on decisions (e.g., choosing a self-hosted issue tracker surfaces "what is the API endpoint and auth model" as a new question).
So after specify, run /speckit.clarify again. If it finds markers, answer them and re-run specify. Repeat until clarify reports nothing outstanding and a read-through of spec.md finds nothing that is not a decision you made. Two or three rounds is normal; one round is normal only if you said no to every extension and your integration answers were already concrete.
Do not proceed to plan with markers remaining. A [NEEDS CLARIFICATION] that survives into /speckit.plan becomes a guess baked into your design.
/speckit.plan       # technical design satisfying the spec
/speckit.tasks      # ordered, dependency-aware build backlog
/speckit.implement  # work through it
After significant milestones, run /speckit.analyze to cross-check spec, plan, tasks, and co

report.summary: Cisco's Advanced Security Initiatives Group published Foundry, a deliberately code-free open specification describing how to build a trustworthy agentic AI security evaluation system on your own stack.
report.background: LLM coding agents have moved from autocomplete to autonomous vulnerability hunting, but most security teams lack a proven architecture for turning a frontier model into a system that produces findings they can trust. Cisco's Advanced Security Initiatives Group ran such an evaluation internally across several iterations and deployment models, accumulating design decisions that mattered and many that did not. Foundry distills that experience into an organization-neutral blueprint. It builds on CodeGuard, a detection rule format Cisco open-sourced earlier and donated to the Coalition for Secure AI (CoSAI), now maintained as an OASIS open project. The spec is also a product of the spec-driven development trend: it is written to be consumed by spec-kit and similar workflows, where a coding agent interviews you until every open question is resolved against your own infrastructure before any implementation begins.
key_points: The deliverable is a specification, not code — the repository contains none on purpose. Cisco argues its internal implementation was welded to its cloud provider, issue tracker, LLM gateway, deployment platform and severity taxonomy, so publishing it would yield something that runs in exactly one environment: theirs. What transfers is the architecture: agent roles, invariants, quality gates, how findings flow to publication, and what counts as done.

At the center is a detection-to-prevention flywheel. CodeGuard rules sweep every function systematically; exploratory agents hunt alongside for bug classes no rule yet describes. When exploration confirms a miss, Foundry records a rule gap, generalizes it into a new or revised rule, and the next sweep catches that entire class on the first pass. Because CodeGuard rules are portable, the same corpus can load into a developer's coding assistant as secure-coding rules, so each evaluation improves prevention everywhere.

It is built for spec-driven development. You copy constitution.md and spec.md into a spec-kit project in Claude Code or a compatible agent, then run /speckit.clarify, which turns roughly three dozen [NEEDS CLARIFICATION] markers into interview questions resolved against your environment. Cisco warns you to loop clarify and specify until no markers remain, because a marker that survives into planning becomes a guess baked into your design.

Cisco is explicit about the audience and the non-goal. Foundry is not a turnkey scanner you pip install and point at a repo. It targets security teams with frontier LLM access, platform teams building internal evaluation capability who prefer a proven shape to a blank page, and researchers who want a reference architecture grounded in production operation rather than benchmarks.

The constitution is treated as accumulated scar tissue. Each principle carries a why-this-is-inviolable paragraph describing the production failure that motivated it. Cisco's guidance: if a principle seems wrong for your situation, the answer is more often that you have not hit that failure yet than that the failure cannot happen there.
report.impact: Foundry signals that agentic security tooling is maturing from demos into architecture. By publishing invariants instead of a product, Cisco pushes standardization onto the layer that actually varies least between organizations, which could accelerate internal builds at companies that would otherwise start from a blank page. For developers, the flywheel idea is the most consequential piece: security findings become a portable rule corpus that feeds coding assistants, collapsing the gap between evaluation and prevention. For regular users, the payoff is indirect but real, since AI-written code increasingly ships behind the products they use. The risk is adoption friction: a code-free spec that demands a frontier LLM, a coding agent, and two or three rounds of clarification will filter out anyone wanting a quick scan.
report.tools: Watch the Foundry spec repository itself, plus three pieces around it: CodeGuard, the detection rule format now maintained as an OASIS open project under the Coalition for Secure AI (CoSAI); spec-kit, GitHub's spec-driven development toolkit, which Foundry is written to be consumed by; and Claude Code or a compatible coding agent to run the clarify, specify, plan, tasks, implement loop. You can also substitute a different rule format entirely, since CodeGuard is a dependency of Foundry's design rather than a requirement.
